{{Short description|General relativity equation}}
{{General relativity |equations}}

In [[physics]], specifically [[general relativity]], the '''Mathisson–Papapetrou–Dixon equations''' describe the motion of a massive spinning body moving in a [[gravitational field]]. Other equations with similar names and mathematical forms are the '''Mathisson–Papapetrou equations''' and '''Papapetrou–Dixon equations'''. All three sets of equations describe the same physics.

These equations are named after [[Myron Mathisson]],<ref>{{cite news |author=M. Mathisson|title=Neue Mechanik materieller Systeme |journal=Acta Physica Polonica |volume=6 |year=1937 |pages=163–209 |url=http://inspirehep.net/record/48323/citations}}</ref> [[William Graham Dixon]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=Dynamics of Extended Bodies in General Relativity. I. Momentum and Angular Momentum |author=W. G. Dixon |year=1970 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1970.0020 |journal=Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A |volume=314 |issue=1519 |bibcode=1970RSPSA.314..499D |pages=499–527|s2cid=119632715 }}</ref> and [[Achilles Papapetrou]],<ref>{{cite journal |author=A. Papapetrou |title=Spinning Test-Particles in General Relativity. I 
|year=1951 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1951.0200 |journal=Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A |volume=209 |issue=1097 
|bibcode=1951RSPSA.209..248P |pages=248–258|s2cid=121464697 
}}</ref> who worked on them.

Throughout, this article uses the [[natural units]] ''c'' = ''G'' = 1, and [[tensor index notation]].

==Mathisson–Papapetrou–Dixon equations==
The Mathisson–Papapetrou–Dixon (MPD) equations for a mass <math>m</math> spinning body are 
:<math>\begin{align}
  \frac{D k_\nu}{D\tau} + \frac 12 S^{\lambda\mu } R_{\lambda \mu\nu \rho}V^\rho &= 0, \\
              \frac{D S^{\lambda\mu}}{D\tau} + V^\lambda k^\mu - V^\mu k^\lambda &= 0.
\end{align}</math>

Here <math>\tau</math> is the proper time along the trajectory, <math>k_\nu</math> is the body's four-momentum
:<math> k_\nu= \int_{t=\text{const}} {T^0}_\nu \sqrt{g} d^3 x,</math> 
the vector <math>V^\mu</math> is the four-velocity of some reference point <math> X^\mu </math> in the body, and the skew-symmetric tensor <math>S^{\mu\nu}</math> is the angular momentum 
:<math>S^{\mu\nu} = \int_{t=\text{const}}\left\{\left(x^\mu - X^\mu\right)T^{0\nu} - \left(x^\nu - X^\nu\right)T^{0\mu}\right\} \sqrt{g}d^3 x</math>
of the body about this point. In the time-slice integrals we are assuming that the body is compact enough that we can use flat coordinates within the body where the energy-momentum tensor <math>T^{\mu\nu}</math> is non-zero.

As they stand, there are only ten equations to determine thirteen quantities. These quantities are the six components of <math>S^{\lambda\mu}</math>, the four components of <math>k_\nu</math> and the three independent components of <math>V^\mu</math>. The equations must therefore be supplemented by three additional constraints which serve to determine which point in the body has velocity <math>V^\mu</math>. Mathison and Pirani originally chose to impose the condition <math>V^\mu S_{\mu\nu} = 0</math> which, although involving four components, contains only three constraints because <math>V^\mu S_{\mu\nu}V^\nu</math> is identically zero. This condition, however, does not lead to a unique solution and can give rise to the mysterious "helical motions".<ref>{{cite journal|title=Mathisson's helical motions demystified|journal=AIP Conf. Proc.|volume=1458 |pages=367–370 |author1=L. F. O. Costa |author2=J. Natário |author3=M. Zilhão |year=2012|arxiv=1206.7093|doi=10.1063/1.4734436|series=AIP Conference Proceedings |bibcode=2012AIPC.1458..367C|s2cid=119306409}}</ref> The Tulczyjew–Dixon condition <math>k_\mu S^{\mu\nu} = 0</math> ''does'' lead to a unique solution as it selects the reference point <math>X^\mu</math> to be the body's center of mass in the frame in which its momentum is <math>(k_0, k_1, k_2, k_3) = (m, 0, 0, 0)</math>.

Accepting the Tulczyjew–Dixon condition <math>k_\mu S^{\mu\nu}=0</math>, we can manipulate the second of the MPD equations into the form 
:<math>\frac{D S_{\lambda\mu }}{D\tau} + \frac 1{m^2}\left(S_{\lambda\rho} k_\mu \frac{D k^\rho}{D\tau} + S_{\rho \mu} k_\lambda \frac{D k^\rho }{D\tau}\right) = 0,</math>

This is a form of Fermi–Walker transport of the spin tensor along the trajectory – but one preserving orthogonality to the momentum vector <math>k^\mu</math> rather than to the tangent vector <math>V^\mu = dX^\mu/d\tau</math>. Dixon calls this ''M-transport''.
